title: Your First Enum
story: You're programming a traffic light for a school project. A light can only be Red, Yellow, or Green — never "purple" or "blinking orange." You need a type that enforces these exact options.
why: Enums define a fixed set of possible values, preventing bugs from invalid inputs and making your code safer.
analogy: An enum is like a multiple-choice question — you can only pick one option from the list. No writing in the margins, no inventing a new answer.
try_it: Add a 'Flashing' variant to the TrafficLight enum. Update the action function to return "Proceed with caution" for Flashing.
tips: Create enum values with `TypeName.Variant` — DOT syntax, like TrafficLight.Red
Variant names use PascalCase: Red, Yellow, Green — same convention as type names
Enums prevent invalid states at compile time — you can't accidentally use TrafficLight.Purple
common_mistakes: Writing `TrafficLight.Red()` with parentheses — simple variants don't have data, so no `()` needed
Comparing with `== "Red"` instead of `== TrafficLight.Red` — enum variants are NOT strings
Forgetting the enum name prefix: `Red` alone won't compile — use `TrafficLight.Red`
